qa_pairs.question: What should C++ developers be aware of regarding compilers and their support for C++ language features and standards?
qa_pairs.answer: C++ developers should understand that different compilers implement various C++ language features uniquely, and specific compiler releases may only partially implement a given ISO C++ standard. For detailed information on which compiler versions support particular language features, developers can consult the cppreference.com wiki page on compiler support.

qa_pairs.question: How do C++ compilers typically handle the C++ Standard Library on Linux systems, and what critical advice is given regarding library paths?
qa_pairs.answer: On Linux systems, many C++ compilers do not provide their own implementation of the C++ Standard Library. Instead, they typically use one already installed on the system, most commonly libstdc++, which is distributed with GCC. Users are strongly advised never to hard-code paths to administrator-installed libraries when compiling software, as this can lead to issues if multiple versions of GCC (and therefore libstdc++) are present on the system.

qa_pairs.question: What significant change occurred in the GCC C++ ABI, and how does it affect linking with older binaries or libraries?
qa_pairs.answer: A major change to the GCC C++ Application Binary Interface (ABI) was introduced during the transition from GCC version 4.9 to 5.1. This change can cause linking to fail if different compiler versions are used, especially when linking to precompiled libraries provided in a vendor's product. To properly link with legacy libraries built with an older ABI, users can employ GCC's Dual ABI feature by passing `-D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0` to GCC if using version 5.1 or higher. Generally, it is recommended to either use the same compiler for all components or recompile older binaries from source with the newer compiler due to frequent C++ ABI updates.
